# Grantha Heritage Tracker: thematic discovery through unsupervised clustering

Problem **SIH26096** · Section **K3P24XC** · CO2 & CO3 · Units III & IV · every number from `reports/deliverable_facts.json`

## 1. Data and scale (Rubric Column 1)

**Q 1.1. Where does the dataset come from, and how big is it? **

15,288 books from the Digital Library of India scans on the Internet Archive, in 8 languages; 13,342 pass the usability gate.

- **Harvest:** a fleet of Google Cloud VMs, one per language (Kannada and Tamil shared one), downloading single pages, never whole PDFs. 76,439 pages were read with Tesseract.
- **Per language (usable of harvested):** English 1,970 of 2,000; Bengali 1,927 of 2,000; Gujarati 1,883 of 2,000; Hindi 1,804 of 2,000; Sanskrit 1,562 of 2,000; Kannada 1,459 of 1,608; Tamil 1,416 of 1,766; Telugu 1,321 of 1,914.

**If an examiner asks:** *Why not NDLI directly?* NDLI aggregates catalogue records and has no bulk API; the Digital Library of India scans are the files behind many of its records.

**Q 1.2. What is the usability gate, and how many books fail it? **

Word-weighted mean OCR confidence ≥ 50 and at least 100 clean tokens. 1,946 books (12.7%) fail.

usable = (mean_conf ≥ 50) ∧ (clean_tokens ≥ 100)

usable 13,342 · excluded 1,946 · splits train 8,005 / val 2,668 / test 2,669

**If an examiner asks:** *Why drop books?* Gibberish OCR creates false closeness between unrelated books. Excluded books stay in the database, flagged, so the decision can be revisited.

**Q 1.3. How are books split for evaluation? **

By a hash of each book's identifier: 60% train, 20% validation, 20% test, the same for a book forever.

- Every fitting step (stopwords, PCA, centring, clustering, DBSCAN eps) sees the train books only.
- An earlier version shuffled the whole corpus; when the corpus grew, held-out books became training books. The hash fixes that, and the change is logged as a deviation in `docs/evaluation_log.md`.

## 2. Preprocessing and vectors (Rubric Column 1)

**Q 2.1. How was OCR done? **

Tesseract 5 LSTM (--oem 1 --psm 3) with orientation and script detection; if the detected script disagrees with the catalogue, both models read the page and the more confident one wins.

- Text used for clustering: the archive's own whole-book OCR for 0 books; our 5 Tesseract pages for 13,342 books with no archive text.

**Q 2.2. Which variables were kept or dropped? **

Kept: text, script, year (median-imputed plus a missing flag), log pages, OCR confidence, log tokens. Dropped: scanning centre and source library (provenance leakage), subject field, free-text fields.

Numeric fields are standardised so year (hundreds) does not outweigh confidence (tens); script is one-hot encoded.

**Q 2.3. How are books turned into vectors, and why centre by language? **

Vertex AI Multilingual embeddings (text-multilingual-embedding-002, 768-d): up to 10 evenly spaced 64-word chunks per book, averaged; each language's mean vector subtracted; PCA to 100 dims.

μℓ = mean of the train books in language ℓ

x̃ = (x − μℓ(x)) / ‖x − μℓ(x)‖

## 3. Hierarchical clustering (Unit III, Rubric Column 2)

**Q 3.1. Compare the four linkages. **

Cophenetic correlation on all books: average 0.485, complete 0.398, Ward 0.396, single 0.036.
| Linkage | Merges by | Behaviour here |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ward | least increase in within-group variance | compact groups of similar size |
| Complete | largest pairwise distance | sensitive to outlying books |
| Average | mean pairwise distance | between the two |
| Single | smallest pairwise distance | chains books one by one; unusable for topics |

**Q 3.2. How was the final setting chosen? **

By a rule fixed before any results, on the train books: ward linkage, euclidean, k = 3. Rule not met; the pre-registered fallback applied.

highest silhouette among feature sets and valid settings whose groups follow script with NMI <= 0.5 and whose median bootstrap ARI >= 0.5. Fallback if nothing passes: the setting with the lowest script NMI, reported as a rule failure.

silhouette 0.040 · script NMI 0.018 · bootstrap ARI 0.24 (20 resamples of 80%)

**If an examiner asks:** *Why is silhouette so low?* Books on one subject vary a lot in vocabulary, so groups overlap; silhouette near zero is common for text. We judge the groups by held-out subject accuracy instead.

## 4. DBSCAN (Unit IV, Rubric Column 2)

**Q 4.1. How were eps and MinPts chosen, and what does noise mean? **

Sorted k-distance curves set the eps range; 24 settings were run; best silhouette among valid ones: eps 0.866, MinPts 20: 2 clusters, 42.4% noise.

- Noise (-1) = a book with fewer than MinPts neighbours within eps, and not near a core book.
- Agreement with the hierarchical groups on non-noise books: ARI -0.001.

**If an examiner asks:** *Why is the catalogue hierarchical, not DBSCAN?* It assigns every book; DBSCAN's verdict is shown next to it in the app as 'in a dense region' or 'noise'.

## 5. PCA (CO3, Rubric Column 2)

**Q 5.1. What does PCA do here, and how much variance is kept? **

PCA reduces 768 → 100 dims for clustering (keeps 78.0%); for display, PC1 11.0%, PC2 8.5%, PC3 5.6% of the 100-d variance.

Σ = (1/N) XᵀX on centred X; Σ vi = λi vi; share of PC i = λi / Σλ

**If an examiner asks:** *Only 19.5% in 2D?* Topics spread over many directions, so a 2D view always shows overlap. We use PCA rather than t-SNE/UMAP because it does not invent gaps.

## 6. Evaluation (Rubric Column 3)

**Q 6.1. How did you check that the groups mean something? **

On 118 labelled test books, each group's majority subject is right 47.5% of the time vs 42.4% for the best simple guess (p = 0.0005, 2,000 label shuffles).
| Target (fixed in advance) | Validation | Test | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1: a page lands with its own book (≥ 80%) | 78.8% | 79.1% | missed |
| T2: subject accuracy vs best baseline (≥ +10 pts) | +8.2 | +5.1 | missed |
| T3: bootstrap ARI (≥ 0.60) | 0.23 | 0.23 | missed |

Test numbers were measured once. Labels come from titles, catalogue fields and an OCR snippet, made with an AI assistant for the team to spot-check; they never form or choose groups.

**If an examiner asks:** *Is this supervised?* No. Clustering never sees a label; labels only measure the groups afterwards.

**Q 6.2. How does this compare with your earlier study? **

The earlier Gemini Embedding study (average, k = 6, fewer books) reached 58.7% subject accuracy, +10.7 points over its baseline.

More books with a different encoder did not give better topics; we report both rather than only the better one.

## 7. Groups and limits (Rubric Column 3)

**Q 7.1. What are the groups? **

3 groups; each named by the majority subject of its labelled train books.
| Group | Books | Majority subject | Largest languages |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group 1 | 6,786 | literature | eng 18%, ben 17%, kan 13% |
| Group 2 | 2,329 | religion and philosophy | tam 20%, guj 16%, san 15% |
| Group 3 | 4,227 | literature | hin 17%, eng 15%, guj 15% |

**Q 7.2. What are the limits, and how does the app behave responsibly? **

Weak stability, AI-assisted labels, uneven OCR quality by language, and an online closed encoder. The app abstains below 20 readable words and shows its evidence.

- Cautions when OCR confidence
- Every answer lists the five nearest archive books, how far the page is from its group's centre relative to the group's own spread, and DBSCAN's verdict.
